findings.figures: Assumed pay inflation: 2.5% per annum for Local Government staff and teaching staff. No contingency provided for higher awards.
findings.quote: This has the potential to change significantly the projected deficit towards the end of the planning period.

findings.headline: Council faces £1.2m increase in Fire Authority levy over three years (from £600k to £1,800k), independently set by Fire Authority with no council control, described as 'obliged to fund.'
findings.detail: The council has no discretion over the Fire Authority levy; it is independently decided and the council is legally obliged to pay increases in full. Over the MTFP period, this levy rises from £600k (2027/28) to £1,800k (2029/30), a £1.2m cumulative increase. This is a known but uncontrollable cost escalation that erodes the council's savings programme.
findings.matters: A lender sees an uncontrollable cost that the council cannot negotiate, defer, or avoid. It reduces the council's flexibility to manage its own finances and pre-commits resources to a third party's spending decisions.
findings.quote: The Council is obliged to fund any increase in levies from the Fire Authority, the Corporate Joint Committee and Swansea Bay Port Health Authority.

findings.headline: Council's capital programme depends on capital receipts materializing; if receipts do not materialize, only alternatives are service cuts or additional borrowing.
findings.detail: The capital strategy explicitly assumes capital receipts will be achieved. Paragraph 36 states: "should such capital receipts not materialise the Council will have no option but to consider reductions in spend, seek alternative sources of funding or, as a last resort, consider additional borrowing which shall place a further burden on revenue finances." The council is betting on property sales and receipts in a soft property market, with no contingency other than more borrowing.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are unpredictable in the short term. If the council's property sales do not proceed as planned, it either cuts services immediately or increases external borrowing, both of which worsen financial resilience.
findings.figures: Capital programme includes Sustainable Communities for Learning £417m investment (£112m locally funded), Swansea Bay City Deal schemes, and others; exact capital receipts target not specified in the MTFP but is material to the plan's balance.
findings.quote: should such capital receipts not materialise the Council will have no option but to consider reductions in spend, seek alternative sources of funding or, as a last resort, consider additional borrowing which shall place a further burden on revenue finances.

findings.headline: Schools hold highest collective reserves of any local authority in Wales but council explicitly states this position is 'not sustainable' without additional Welsh Government funding.
findings.detail: Paragraph 84 states: "Our schools are in the privileged position of having the current highest collective reserves of any local authority in Wales." However, it immediately warns: "that position is not sustainable and it will provide a natural brake on the ability to expect schools to make further budget savings without wholescale redesign." Schools are expected to spend reserves in the short term but this is acknowledged as a temporary solution. The plan assumes only small schools savings requests for the MTFP period, but also notes: "the medium-term impact is that this will significantly impact Schools unless significant additional funding is forthcoming."
findings.matters: A lender understands that reserve-spending buys time, not solvency. Swansea's school sector is one spending shock away from forced service reductions, and the council acknowledges this will happen unless Welsh Government increases schools funding.
findings.figures: School reserves described as highest collective level in Wales. No specific figure given for schools reserves or the depletion timeline.
findings.quote: that position is not sustainable and it will provide a natural brake on the ability to expect further savings contributions. The clear aim is to support and protect schools in the short-term as much as possible, however the medium-term impact is that this will significantly impact Schools unless significant additional funding is forthcoming from the Welsh (and ultimately UK) Government.

findings.headline: Council locked in historic all-time low PWLB borrowing rates from 2021/22; borrowing costs forecast to rise significantly from 2029/30 onwards.
findings.detail: The council took advantage of all-time low PWLB rates in 2021/22 to borrow for capital schemes. The plan now forecasts that borrowing costs will show "a gradual increase from 2026/27 until 2029/30 when a significant increase in borrowing costs is expected." The council has £50m general borrowing and £25m Mumbles coastal defence borrowing already deferred. If interest rates remain elevated beyond 2029/30, revenue financing costs could exceed plan assumptions.
findings.matters: A council's borrowing costs are its largest fixed-term commitment. Rising rates from 2029/30 mean either higher revenue costs or deferred capital schemes. This constrains the council's financial flexibility precisely when the savings programme is most demanding.
findings.figures: £50m general deferred borrowing; £25m Mumbles CMRP coastal defence deferred borrowing; £22m Minimum Revenue Provision annually for debt repayment.
findings.quote: gradual increase from 2026/27 until 2029/30 when a significant increase in borrowing costs is expected to deliver the full externalisation of only the currently agreed deferred borrowing (£50m general and £25m Mumbles CMRP coastal defence scheme).

findings.headline: Unquantified equal pay liability explicitly identified as ongoing risk with no financial provision made.
findings.detail: The plan lists equal pay claims and review work as an ongoing, unresolved issue but makes no provision for costs. This is mentioned twice as a material risk. The S151 Officer acknowledges it could have future implications but has not modelled any cost impact, leaving the true financial position potentially materially understated.
findings.matters: Equal pay settlements can be large, back-dated, and move quickly. A council with unresolved equal pay risk has an unquantified contingent liability that could force emergency budget action.
findings.figures: None quantified in the plan.
findings.quote: Any ongoing implications that may arise from the equal pay claims and review work currently underway.

findings.headline: Escalating savings requirement depends entirely on unconfirmed 2% annual Welsh Government funding increases; if funding is flat (0%), council needs £29.6m additional savings over three years.
findings.detail: The plan balances only if AEF (Aggregate External Finance) grows 2% annually. The Welsh Government has confirmed funding only for 2026/27; no guidance given for future years. The plan explicitly states: if AEF turns out to be 0%, the additional savings needed would be £9.7m (2027/28), £19.6m (2028/29), and £29.6m (2029/30). At 4% growth, there would instead be a £31m surplus. This represents a £60m swing in the financial position based on a single assumption.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the balanced budget is robust or hangs on a funding guess. If settlements prove lower, the council faces immediate, mid-plan choices between uncontrolled borrowing or emergency service cuts.
findings.figures: Cumulative Savings Requirement: £8,309k (2027/28), £17,474k (2028/29), £18,271k (2029/30). If AEF 0%: additional savings needed £9,700k, £19,600k, £29,600k respectively. If AEF 4%: surplus available £10,000k, £20,000k, £31,000k.
findings.quote: The compounding effect of this key assumption is substantial over the life of the MTFP – the savings ask could be considerably higher if the actual increase is less than the range used as a planning assumption or considerably less if the settlements are more than assumed.

findings.headline: Finance costs rising by £813k due to increased borrowing for capital investment
findings.detail: Capital financing charges will increase by £813k in 2026/27 due to the council delivering its largest capital programme to date in response to WHQS requirements and More Homes Programme obligations. The council notes this increase was anticipated given the economic climate.
findings.matters: Rising capital finance costs indicate the council is borrowing heavily to meet statutory housing obligations; this increases fixed debt service costs and reduces flexibility if cost pressures return to HRA operations.
findings.figures: Finance costs increase £813k in 2026/27; capital programme £69.5m
findings.quote: Capital Financing Charges – These will increase in 2026/27 which was anticipated given the current economic climate and line with delivering our largest capital budget programme to date.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage from £56m to £54m with risk of further deterioration
findings.detail: The HRA's capital budget has been reduced from £56m to £54m due to natural slippage, with the possibility of additional slippage. This occurs whilst the council is planning its largest capital budget programme to date (£69.5m in 2026/27) and pursuing the More Homes Programme, suggesting delivery capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Repeated capital delivery slippage indicates project management or funding constraints; it delays asset maintenance and new affordable housing delivery, extending the HRA's exposure to further inflationary cost pressures.
findings.figures: Capital budget reduced from £56m to £54m; 2026/27 capital programme £69.5m; revenue contribution to capital £30.2m
findings.quote: Capital budgets have been reduced from £56m to £54m due to natural slippage with the possibility of this slippage increasing slightly

findings.headline: New statutory housing standards (WHQS 2023) explicitly stated as unaffordable without external subsidy
findings.detail: The Welsh Housing Quality Standard 2023 imposes new mandatory investment requirements with no additional external funding from Welsh Government. The council faces three competing statutory/policy priorities: maintaining existing stock condition, increasing affordable housing supply (to address homelessness crisis), and meeting WHQS 2023 compliance. The council explicitly states these cannot all be delivered.
findings.matters: A statutory obligation that the council explicitly says cannot be afforded creates covenant breach risk, suggests borrowing will be required for compliance, and flags delivery failure if rent income does not grow or if cost inflation continues.
findings.figures: WHQS 2023 requires significant extra investment; no funding gap quantified
findings.quote: Unless more income from rent can be achieved or there is significant funding from Welsh Government these requirements are unaffordable and cannot be delivered in full.

findings.headline: Largest investment programme (QED/Schools circa £400m) not fully approved; subject to Welsh Government review in 2027
findings.detail: The QED/Sustainable Communities for Learning programme represents the largest component of the capital programme. Welsh Government approval was only given 'in principle' for years 1-6 in August 2024, and the SOP is subject to preparation for the next WG review in 2027. Individual projects require further WG approval and business case development.
findings.matters: Funding uncertainty on the largest programme creates delivery risk. WG funding conditions could change, forcing scope reduction, deferral, or forcing the council to fund gaps from its own resources.
findings.figures: QED programme circa £400m overall; current profile £371.723m; WG approval 'in principle' only for years 1-6
findings.quote: Each of the investment priorities will be subject to detailed business case development and further WG approvals, together with separate reports to Cabinet for decision.

findings.headline: Capital receipts funding risk: only £6.485m planned from a £654m programme over six years
findings.detail: General fund capital receipts of just £6.485m are planned to fund 1% of the total six-year programme. The risk table identifies 'General fund capital receipts do not materialise at the level planned' as a key risk with impact of 'Funding shortfall', meaning any shortfall would require additional borrowing to fill the gap.
findings.matters: Low planned receipts means the programme is almost entirely dependent on external grants and borrowing. Any failure to realize planned asset sales will force additional unplanned borrowing or project deferral.
findings.figures: £6.485m capital receipts planned vs £653.952m total programme (0.99%)
findings.quote: General fund capital receipts do not materialise at the level planned | Funding shortfall

findings.headline: Revenue budget already under strain, limiting council's ability to absorb additional capital financing costs
findings.detail: The paper explicitly references an 'already challenging revenue budget scenario' and states that additional capital financing costs risk impacting this constrained revenue position. This suggests the council has limited headroom to absorb rising debt service costs from the £168m borrowing programme.
findings.matters: If revenue budgets cannot absorb rising debt service, the council will face service cuts or further borrowing, creating a vicious cycle. A lender needs to know whether debt service is sustainable from operating revenue.
findings.figures: No specific reserve figures, but programme assumes costs supportable from 'likely future revenue budgets affordably and sustainably'
findings.quote: any capital expenditure that leads to an overall net increase in borrowing costs brings with it the potential to impact on an already challenging revenue budget scenario going forward.

findings.headline: Capital governance weaknesses identified in WLGA peer review; new oversight board launching March 2026
findings.detail: The council's capital governance has come under external peer review by WLGA. Recommendations are being implemented during 2026/27, including launch of a new capital oversight board in March 2026. This indicates previously identified governance gaps in capital planning and delivery.
findings.matters: Weak capital governance historically correlates with cost overruns, poor project selection, and wasted capital investment. The requirement for remedial action signals prior control deficiencies.
findings.figures: New capital oversight board launching March 2026
findings.quote: The councils capital governance is currently under review following the WLGA Peer Review. Work will soon conclude on addressing the recommendation from the review to strengthen capital governance and capital planning. A new capital oversight board will be launched in March 2026

findings.headline: Unsupported borrowing requirement of £168.078m over six years with financing costs forecast to be materially higher than recent past
findings.detail: The capital programme of £653.952m requires £168.078m in unsupported borrowing. The paper explicitly forecasts that financing costs will be materially higher than previously because of higher gilt yields. This constrains the council's policy choices and limits capital capacity available for discretionary investment.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt trajectory and the rising cost of debt service. Material increases in financing costs reduce the revenue available for service delivery and signal exposure to interest rate risk.
findings.figures: £168.078m unsupported borrowing requirement; £653.952m total programme; £654m with £50m headroom envelope
findings.quote: The costs of financing the same are forecast to be materially higher than the recent past noting the higher gilt yield environment, which in turn may limit the capital secured for any policy choice over the balance between revenue and capital priorities.

findings.headline: S151 Officer explicitly warns of revenue constraints limiting ability to service additional borrowing
findings.detail: The S151 Officer states that 'capital resource and importantly the revenue resources available to support any borrowing are both limited and finite' and references recent examples (Woking, Spelthorne) where 'overstretched, flawed capital programmes' resulted in S114 notices (formal financial failure declarations).
findings.matters: When a finance officer of a borrowing council explicitly warns of constrained revenue capacity, it signals genuine budget pressure and risk of future inability to service debt or fund services.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: it needs to be recognised that capital resource and importantly the revenue resources available to support any borrowing are both limited and finite. The robustness of the capital financing strategy is paramount in light of recent countless examples (Woking, Spelthorne) in local authorities in England where overstretched, flawed capital programmes has resulted in the issuance of a S.114 Notice

findings.headline: Major regeneration schemes anchored in City Deal extend financial obligations to 2032/33
findings.detail: The £1.3bn Swansea Bay City Deal regional programme runs until 2032/33, with major projects (Swansea Arena, Digital Village, UWTSD innovation facilities) already delivered and operational but generating ongoing revenue implications through management, maintenance and debt servicing.
findings.matters: Long-term regional commitments limit financial flexibility and create multi-decade revenue exposure even after capital delivery is complete; any deterioration in project performance affects revenue.
findings.figures: £1.3bn regional programme; individual project occupancy: 80% for Digital Village, ongoing visitor numbers for Arena
findings.quote: The Swansea Bay City Deal is a regional £1.3bn programme. The Swansea Bay City Deal Joint Committee remains in place until the full regional portfolio (nine projects) concludes and the benefit realisation period has concluded 2032/33

findings.headline: Governance review of capital delivery planned for 2026/27 following peer review
findings.detail: The council indicates that a peer review exercise has been completed and a governance review is planned for 2026/27. Currently, capital delivery is overseen by multiple boards (Regeneration, Housing Futures, Sustainable Communities for Learning) plus quarterly budget monitoring, contract procedure rules and financial procedure rules.
findings.matters: A governance review after external scrutiny suggests previous issues with capital management or project delivery; lenders should watch for findings and remediation.
findings.figures: Not applicable
findings.quote: there is a planned review of the corporate governance surrounding capital delivery in 2026/27 following a Peer Review exercise

findings.headline: Hundreds of millions in potential future capital requirements not yet funded or planned for
findings.detail: Beyond the approved capital programme, the council identifies 'potential substantial investments' for business continuity and statutory compliance (including sustainable learning communities and carbon zero obligations) that 'could lead to capital requirements in the hundreds of millions' but are 'definitively not afforded or factored into the medium or indeed longer term financial plans at this stage'.
findings.matters: Unfunded statutory compliance requirements create future budget shock and present a sustainability risk; they may force borrowing or service cuts within the medium-term planning horizon.
findings.figures: Hundreds of millions (unquantified)
findings.quote: Beyond these agreed projects there are also potential substantial investments that whilst only estimated at this stage, could lead to capital requirements in the hundreds of millions for not just Corporate Objectives but also to deliver business continuity or statutory compliance

findings.headline: Rising interest rates materially increasing cost of servicing capital programme
findings.detail: The council notes borrowing costs are 'forecast to be materially higher than the recent past noting the higher gilt yield environment'. The council previously took advantage of historically cheap PWLB rates (£90m in 2018/19 and £120m in 2021/22 at average 1.94%, described as 'cheapest borrowing ever undertaken by this Council'). Current rates are substantially higher, making future borrowing significantly more expensive.
findings.matters: Rising interest rates directly increase revenue costs of existing capital programme and make any new borrowing less affordable; this constrains both future capital investment and service spending.
findings.figures: Historical rates: 1.94% average (2021/22); current: 'materially higher' (not specified)
findings.quote: The costs of financing the same are forecast to be materially higher than the recent past noting the higher gilt yield environment, which in turn may limit the capital secured for any policy choice over the balance between revenue and capital priorities

findings.headline: Housing Quality Standard requires £960m investment but council can only fund prioritised portion
findings.detail: Welsh Housing Quality Standard 2023 compliance requires £960m over ten years to meet energy efficiency, carbon neutrality and other standards. The council admits this is 'unaffordable' and has created a prioritised programme (contractual obligations, maintenance, sustainability duties) that excludes full compliance. Decarbonisation work is only funded if Welsh Government provides specific grants.
findings.matters: A £960m unfunded capital need creates future budget pressure and regulatory risk; failure to meet housing standards could trigger intervention or enforcement action.
findings.figures: £960m required; only prioritised portion funded in current programme
findings.quote: In September 2025 an exercise was undertaken to understand the long-term capital investment needed to fully meet the standard. It is estimated the Council will require £960m to meet all aspects of the standard in the next 10 years. Because this is unaffordable and the available capital investment is insufficient, the programme presented in this report is prioritised

findings.headline: £168.078m unsupported borrowing requirement across 6-year capital programme
findings.detail: The council's capital programme totals £653.952m with £168.078m requiring unsupported borrowing (not covered by grant or receipts). This is described as 'significant' and requires substantial revenue funding to service the finance costs. The S151 Officer emphasises that revenue resources available to support borrowing are 'limited and finite'.
findings.matters: This scale of borrowing ties up a council's revenue budget for decades and limits flexibility to respond to service pressures or respond to new demands.
findings.figures: £653.952m total programme; £168.078m unsupported borrowing requirement
findings.quote: The updated total Capital programme which includes a 5 year forward expenditure programme plus current year of £653.952m identifying an unsupported borrowing requirement of £168.078m

findings.headline: UK Shared Prosperity Fund unwinding creates specific grant funding cliff
findings.detail: The S151 Officer warns: 'In particular in 2026/27 there will be a significant risk around the UK Shared Prosperity Fund as it begins to unwind. A further report to Cabinet in March is expected to accommodate the Local Growth Fund changes and targeted local additional support from the Council's own resources.' The SPF is being replaced with more capital-focused funding, requiring local top-up that does not fully replace what was lost.
findings.matters: Falling grant income forces budget reductions or reserves drawdown. SPF unwinding is not within the council's control.
findings.figures: £10m Economic Growth Fund being ring-fenced from contingency; SPF phasing out (specific amount not quantified in extract)
findings.quote: In particular in 2026/27 there will be a significant risk around the UK Shared Prosperity Fund as it begins to unwind... funding has reduced and will be more capital based, there will be a local top up to replace some of the funding but not all

findings.headline: Use of Capital Equalisation Reserve to balance revenue budget is non-standard and temporary
findings.detail: The S151 Officer flags a significant policy deviation: 'In 2025/26, for the first time, the revenue budget was predicated on drawing sums from the Capital Equalisation reserve solely for the purposes of balancing revenue pressures not to solely smooth the cost of capital financing in revenue. This is also built into the 2026/27 budget although there is an exit strategy built into the Medium Term Financial Plan. This is a deviation from previously agreed Council policy and is not considered by the S151 Officer to be strategic in deployment of reserves for their intended purposes.' They explicitly modify their Section 25 assurance on this point.
findings.matters: Using capital reserves for revenue is a sign of structural budget stress and reduces financial flexibility for capital investment.
findings.figures: Capital Equalisation Reserve drawn to support revenue (amount not specified in this extract)
findings.quote: This is a deviation from previously agreed Council policy and is not considered by the S151 Officer to be strategic in deployment of reserves for their intended purposes... The Section 25 assurance is consequently once again explicitly modified and qualified

findings.headline: Capital financing charges rising and borrowing more expensive in new rate environment
findings.detail: Capital financing charges increase from £33.894m (2025/26) to £34.894m (2026/27). The S151 Officer states 'the current market and inflationary environment, makes funding the capital programme even more challenging' and notes that 'financing costs more than doubling in the interim' since historically low rates secured in 2018/19 and 2021/22. PWLB borrowing is now materially more expensive and the council is exploring alternative sources including local authorities, financial institutions, and Municipal Bonds Agency.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs compress the budget and limit flexibility. If capital plans proceed, borrowing costs will worsen further.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Charges: £33.894m (2025/26) to £34.894m (2026/27), increase of £1.0m
findings.quote: The current market and inflationary environment, makes funding the capital programme even more challenging... financing costs more than doubling in the interim

findings.headline: Equal pay provision of £15m may be inadequate as further claims emerge
findings.detail: The council prudently set aside £15m for equal pay claims in 2023/24. However, the S151 Officer explicitly states 'Further claims are being made on other aspects of equal pay. Work is on-going to determine if this provision should be increased and if so by how much.' These risks are 'disclosed in the accounts as an additional potentially material contingent liability only', suggesting the £15m may not cover future exposure.
findings.matters: Equal pay claims are a known liability affecting many councils, and Swansea's exposure could be larger than currently reserved. This affects balance sheet strength.
findings.figures: £15m base provision for equal pay; further claims disclosed as contingent liability
findings.quote: Further claims are being made on other aspects of equal pay. Work is on-going to determine if this provision should be increased and if so by how much. Legal and other external advice is being sought.

findings.headline: General reserves at absolute minimum with no route back if they are drawn
findings.detail: The S151 Officer states that General Reserves stand at £14.0m (2% of budgeted net spending) and describes this as 'the very minimum level' and 'the absolute minimum safe level'. They explicitly warn that 'both those routes are now all but fully exhausted going forward' - meaning neither General Reserves nor Earmarked Reserves can be used to fund future budget shortfalls. The S151 Officer advises that Council will face the choice between service reductions, capital reductions, council tax increases, or one-off draws from time-limited earmarked reserves 'with an explicit acceptance and understanding that these are one off mitigations only'.
findings.matters: Depletion of reserves is a key credit signal. A council without reserves has no shock absorber and becomes more dependent on swift achievement of savings plans.
findings.figures: General Reserves £14.0m at 2% of budgeted spend; Contingency Fund £8.594m; total Earmarked Reserves forecast at -£115.116m
findings.quote: In the opinion of the S151 Officer the level of the General Reserve is currently at the very minimum level (at 2% of net budgeted spend)... both those routes are now all but fully exhausted going forward

findings.headline: Property investment strategy now constrained by CIPFA guidance preventing yield-only acquisitions
findings.detail: CIPFA guidance now prevents councils from borrowing to acquire properties purely for investment yield, forcing the council to abandon its previous strategy of generating additional revenue through property acquisitions.
findings.matters: Loss of a primary strategy for generating alternative revenue reduces financial flexibility and future income sources.
findings.figures: Current non-operational investment portfolio generates c.£8.5m annually (excluding Quadrant)
findings.quote: Whilst the Property Investment Strategy continues to be a key focus for the Council, the overall approach has shifted due to recent CIPFA guidance which prevents local authorities buying property investments purely for yield. The key constraint is that a Council must not borrow money purely for the sake of making a profit greater than their borrowing costs.

findings.headline: Wales Audit Office flagged asset management governance gaps in April 2024
findings.detail: Audit found the council needs to improve understanding of asset conditions and risks, enhance partnership working, and establish effective monitoring of asset management activities.
findings.matters: External audit identified governance weaknesses in financial asset management and regulatory compliance oversight.
findings.figures: Wales Audit Office report, April 2024
findings.quote: The overall conclusion was that the Council is using its assets to meet strategic goals but needs to improve its understanding of asset conditions and risks, enhance partnership working, and establish more effective monitoring of asset management activities.

findings.headline: Only 17% of required asset condition surveys completed, data gaps limiting maintenance prioritisation
findings.detail: The council is conducting a 5-year rolling condition survey programme of approximately 700 corporate buildings. Fewer than 120 surveys have been completed, meaning capital maintenance priorities are currently allocated ad-hoc without full asset condition understanding.
findings.matters: Incomplete asset data prevents evidence-based maintenance prioritisation, increases risk of missing critical failures, and indicates weak financial governance.
findings.figures: c.700 condition surveys required; c.120 completed; 4 years remaining; 7-year investment plans being established for 8 strategic assets
findings.quote: It will take a further 4 years to complete all c.700 condition surveys, so in the meantime, 7 year investment plans are being established for the Council's strategic assets.

findings.headline: Declining capital receipts from property disposals due to site constraints
findings.detail: The council's capital programme relies on income from selling surplus property. The report warns that disposal opportunities are reducing because of finite site supply, planning constraints, and viability issues, leading to projected lower capital receipts in future years.
findings.matters: Loss of disposal income reduces capital funding capacity and creates uncertainty in capital planning.
findings.figures: Receipts from disposal programme currently assists Corporate Capital programme; expected to decline
findings.quote: Receipts from the disposal programme currently assists the Corporate Capital programme. However, a finite supply of sites, competition from the internal market, onerous planning/regulatory conditions, and general site constraints leads to viability issues that reduce the number of sites which the council are able to bring forward in future years with a corresponding reduction in capital receipt from sales.

findings.headline: Council unable to fund capital maintenance to safe and compliant levels
findings.detail: The report explicitly names this as "the biggest issue" facing the authority. Capital maintenance budget has been flatlined while materials and labour costs have significantly increased, creating an inability to maintain buildings to safe and compliant standards.
findings.matters: Underfunded asset maintenance creates health and safety liabilities, increases emergency repair costs, and signals structural financial stress.
findings.figures: Capital maintenance budget: £3.2m per annum (flatlined); revenue maintenance: £2.7m per annum
findings.quote: the biggest issue that now face is the authority over the life of this asset management plan is the inability to fund capital maintenance to the point of the provision of a safe and compliant portfolio.

findings.headline: The council's overall reserve adequacy depends entirely on earmarked reserves; if these fall, the General Fund would need to increase substantially.
findings.detail: The S151 Officer states that the current reserve level of £157.19m is adequate only because £126.557m is in earmarked reserves committed to specific purposes. The General Fund Balance is £14m and is described as "still below average" as a percentage of Gross Revenue Expenditure. The Capital Equalisation Reserve is also "effectively fully committed over the next few years." The S151 Officer explicitly states that "should [earmarked reserves] fall significantly then the General Reserve will need to be increased."
findings.matters: The council's financial resilience rests on reserves that are largely already assigned to specific schemes or contingencies. Any drawdown of earmarked reserves to cover deficits or unforeseen costs would reveal an underlying inadequacy in the General Fund, which the council has struggled to build despite favourable outturns.
findings.figures: Total usable reserves: £157.19m; General Fund Balance: £14m; Earmarked reserves: £126.557m; of which Capital Equalisation fully committed and Contingency fully pre-committed
findings.quote: the Section 151 Officer accepts the levels to be adequate only because of the high level of earmarked reserves and should these fall significantly then the General Reserve will need to be increased.

findings.headline: The contingency fund of £18.133m is fully pre-committed and will be completely exhausted during 2025/26.
findings.detail: The Contingency Fund balance of £18.133m is described as "pre-committed and expected fully expended in 2025/26 as a result of likely in year Cabinet decisions, including the creation of an Economic Growth Fund." Once this fund is spent, the council will lose a significant buffer for unforeseen costs.
findings.matters: The exhaustion of the contingency fund reduces the council's ability to respond to emergencies or unexpected costs, making it more reliant on either the General Fund Balance (£14m) or accessing earmarked reserves that are designated for other purposes.
findings.figures: Contingency Fund: £18.133m; with £10m diverted to Economic Growth Fund
findings.quote: The brought forward contingency fund is pre-committed and expected fully expended in 2025/26 as a result of likely in year Cabinet decisions, including the creation of an Economic Growth Fund.

findings.headline: The council is planning structural change with "substantial up-front costs" and workforce reductions inevitable.
findings.detail: The council states it needs to "prepare for significant change in service delivery that will inevitably impact on direct employment levels going forward." Cabinet has already committed the Restructure Reserve to funding the Workforce and OD Transformation Programme and Digital Strategy 2023-2028. The S151 Officer describes dealing with the cost of future structural change as "a significant financial risk given the scale and pace of budget pressures to be addressed by the Council."
findings.matters: Transformation costs will be incurred during a period of severe budget constraint and will consume reserves. If transformation does not deliver the expected savings, or if it takes longer than planned, the council's reserves position could deteriorate rapidly.
findings.figures: Restructure Reserve committed to Workforce and OD Transformation and Digital Strategy 2023-2028
findings.quote: Changes on such a scale will inevitably come with substantial up-front costs and it is important at this time that the Council plans operationally and financially to meet these changes. Dealing with the cost of future structural change is a significant financial risk given the scale and pace of budget pressures to be addressed by the Council.

findings.headline: All directorates are expected to find it increasingly hard to live within budgets due to uncontrolled demand in social care, homelessness and ALNET.
findings.detail: The council explicitly recognises that demand pressures on services such as ALNET (Additional Learning Needs Education Tribunal), Social Care and Homelessness will make it "increasingly hard" for all directorates to stay within budget. This is framed as an ongoing operational reality separate from the planned savings requirement.
findings.matters: Demand overspends could cause the council to miss the savings targets it has committed to, requiring reserves to be drawn down ahead of plan or additional borrowing. This compounds the deficit risk already flagged in the Medium-Term Financial Plan.
findings.figures: Services named: ALNET, Social Care, Homelessness
findings.quote: Equally, it is likely that all Directorates will find it increasingly hard to live within budgets primarily due to demand pressures on services such as ALNET, Social Care and Homelessness.

findings.headline: The council faces a cumulative deficit of £61.7m by 2028/29 with an accelerating savings requirement that more recent forecasts suggest will be even larger.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan forecasts a cumulative deficit of £61.7m by 2028/29 with an immediate savings requirement of £11.5m for 2026/27, on top of the current year's £18.5m. The paper notes that "more recent forecasts indicate an even larger savings requirement will be likely by the end of the MTFP period, predominantly as a result of ongoing demographic pressures and the use of temporary one-off funding for 2025/26." Even if all planned 2025/26 savings are achieved, this still leaves a minimum gap of £11.5m for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this scale signals sustained pressure on the council's ability to deliver services and service its debt. The requirement for larger-than-planned savings suggests the council's own forecasting has been conservative, raising questions about whether the planned savings will be delivered.
findings.figures: £61.7m cumulative deficit by 2028/29; £11.5m savings required 2026/27; £18.5m current year savings requirement
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Plan approved by Council on 6th March 2025 forecast a cumulative deficit on General Fund Revenue Expenditure of some £61.7m by 2028/29, based on an average 2% increase in Government funding for 3 years, with an immediate savings requirement of £11.5m for 2026/27. This is in addition to the current year savings requirement of £18.5m. More recent forecasts indicate an even larger savings requirement will be likely by the end of the MTFP period, predominantly as a result of ongoing demographic pressures and the use of temporary one-off funding for 2025/26.

news_drafts.lead: Weak fraud detection frameworks could allow financial irregularities to go undetected, and auditor findings on control adequacy inform lender confidence in the council's governance and financial reporting reliability

news_drafts.lead: Large deferred maintenance backlogs can force sudden, unplanned capital spending that squeezes other priorities. This systematic assessment may reveal how much the Council needs to commit to building maintenance.
